subtype: Feels cheated when kindness is not returned [Receiver]
passage: On Sankranti morning, Urmila lent her best kite, the red one with the long tail, to Darshan from the next house, because his had torn. "Just for one hour," she said. He flew it all afternoon. Later, when Urmila asked to borrow his spool of glass-coated thread for one flight, Darshan said, "No, Appa said not to lend it." Urmila stood on the roof with her mouth open. "But I gave you my kite!" Darshan shrugged. "That was your choice." Urmila marched downstairs, took her kite back without asking and told her mother, "I'm never lending him anything again. Never ever." Her mother noticed her fists were clenched.

qa.q: What colour was Urmila's best kite?
qa.a: Red, with a long tail.

qa.q: Why did Urmila feel so wronged when Darshan said no?
qa.a: She felt cheated and angry: she saw lending as a trade, so after giving her kite she expected something back, and his refusal felt like a broken deal.

qa.q: What could Urmila's mother say to help her?
qa.a: Her mother could agree it hurts when kindness isn't returned, and gently ask whether Darshan might have been following his Appa's rule.

qa.q: How might Darshan see the situation?
qa.a: Darshan may think he did nothing wrong since his Appa said not to lend the thread, and may not realise Urmila expected a return favour.

grounding: A child who lent her kite and was refused a favour in return feels cheated and vows never to lend again.

subtype: Feels cheated when kindness is not returned [Receiver]
passage: Yara had lent her new roller skates to Nkechi for the whole Saturday at the park near their flats in Lagos. On Monday at school, Yara asked to borrow Nkechi's set of glitter pens for her art project. "Sorry, they're new, I don't lend them," Nkechi said, zipping her pencil case. Yara felt her ears get hot. She had cleaned the skates specially before lending them. She walked home fast, kicking a stone. At dinner she announced, "I'm never lending anything to anyone again. People just take." Her older brother laughed, but her mother asked, "Did Nkechi say thank you for the skates?" Yara thought. "Yes. But that's not the same."

qa.q: What did Yara lend Nkechi?
qa.a: Her new roller skates, for the whole Saturday.

qa.q: What does Yara kicking a stone on the way home suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt angry and hurt that Nkechi wouldn't lend the pens after Yara lent her skates.

qa.q: How could Yara's mother build on her question to help Yara?
qa.a: She could say a thank-you still counts for something, and help Yara see that kindness is not always paid back in the same way.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have seen things?
qa.a: Nkechi may not have linked the skates and the pens at all, and simply felt protective of her new pens.

grounding: A child who lent her skates feels cheated when her friend won't lend pens in return, and declares she'll never lend again.

subtype: Feels cheated when kindness is not returned [Receiver]
passage: Every day at the school lunch hall, Ishita shared her aloo paratha with Pranav because he said his tiffin was boring. On Thursday Pranav came with gulab jamuns, four of them, and ate them with two other boys at the next table. He didn't offer Ishita even one. Ishita's throat felt tight. She stared at her paratha, then closed her tiffin. When Pranav came over on Friday asking, "Paratha?" she said, "No. You didn't share your gulab jamuns. It's not fair. I'm not sharing anymore." Pranav looked surprised. "They were for my friends." "I thought I was your friend," Ishita said, and turned away.

qa.q: How many gulab jamuns did Pranav bring on Thursday?
qa.a: Four of them.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when Pranav didn't offer her a gulab jamun?
qa.a: She felt hurt and cheated, her throat tight, because she had shared with him every day and got nothing back.

qa.q: What could Ishita do next that is honest without closing the door?
qa.a: She could tell Pranav calmly that she felt left out, and see how he responds, rather than stopping all sharing forever.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Ishita's refusal?
qa.a: Pranav seems surprised, as he may not have realised she expected a share or that she saw herself as his friend.

grounding: A child who shared lunch every day feels wronged when her friend does not share back and refuses to share again.

passage:
I'm Mansi, Tavish's big sister. Last month Tavish, nine, lent his remote-control car to Kartik from the next flat for a whole weekend. He was proud about it. He kept saying, "I shared my best thing."
When it came back, one antenna was bent and Kartik didn't say sorry. Then on Wednesday, Tavish asked to borrow Kartik's new cricket bat for one match. Kartik said, "No, it's new, my father said not to lend it."
Tavish came home and threw his shoes at the wall. "I gave him my car for two days! He gave me nothing!" His face was red and his voice was shaking. "Never again. I'm never lending anything to anyone."
I tried to say maybe Kartik's father really did say that. Tavish wouldn't listen. He put the car on the top shelf. I think he felt cheated, like someone had broken a rule.

qa.q: What was bent when the car came back?
qa.a: One antenna was bent.

qa.q: Why did Tavish feel so angry after Kartik refused the bat?
qa.a: He saw lending as an exchange, so after giving his best toy for two days, getting nothing back felt like being cheated.

qa.q: What turning point could help Tavish, and what might someone say to him?
qa.a: The moment he said 'never again' is where someone could help him see that Kartik's refusal might be about his father's rule, and that Tavish's own sharing was still a good thing.

qa.q: How might Kartik see this situation?
qa.a: Kartik may think he was only following his father's rule and not realise how unfair it felt to Tavish, especially after the bent antenna.

grounding: It shows, through a sister's eyes, a child who lent a toy and got nothing in return, feeling cheated and declaring he will never lend again.

passage:
Monday. Salma, ten, lent her toy microscope to Elizabeth for the weekend project. "Be careful with the little glass slides," she said. Elizabeth hugged her.
Thursday. Elizabeth gave it back with one slide cracked and said nothing about it. At lunch, Elizabeth had a new set of scented gel pens. Salma asked, "Can I try the purple?" Elizabeth said, "Maybe later," and put them away.
Saturday. Salma sat on her bed turning the cracked slide in her fingers. When her mother asked what was wrong, she burst out, "I gave her my microscope. She won't even give me one pen. That's not fair!" She wiped her eyes angrily. "Never again. Next time I'm saying no."
Ammi sat beside her and didn't argue. She just stroked Salma's hair while Salma cried it out.

qa.q: What was cracked when Elizabeth returned the microscope?
qa.a: One slide was cracked.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling as she turned the cracked slide in her fingers?
qa.a: She felt hurt and cheated, because she had given something precious and Elizabeth would not share even one pen in return.

qa.q: What could Salma's mother help her think about once she is calmer?
qa.a: She could help Salma tell Elizabeth about the cracked slide and how she felt, and see that her own kindness wasn't wasted even if it wasn't returned.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see the gel pens and the microscope?
qa.a: Elizabeth may not have linked the two at all, seeing the new pens as special and not realising Salma expected a fair return.

grounding: It shows over several days a child who lent a toy, got nothing back and a cracked slide, and felt wronged enough to say 'never again'.
